snippets.title: Variables and print
snippets.prompt: Create a variable name set to the text "Ada" and a variable age set to 28, then print both on a single line.
snippets.hint: print(name, age) accepts two arguments and separates them with a space.
snippets.explain: Stores two pieces of information in named variables and then prints both at once. `name` holds text (a string) and `age` holds a whole number (an int). Passing two arguments to print separates the output with a single space: `Ada 28`.
snippets.gotcha: Writing `age = "28"` makes it text, and `age + 1` would then fail with a TypeError.

notes.note: Creates a variable `name` and assigns it the string "Ada". The quotes are part of the syntax, not the value.
Creates `age` and assigns the integer 28 — no quotes, so Python treats it as a number.
print() can take several arguments; it prints them separated by spaces, so this outputs: Ada 28

snippets.title: Check the type of a value
snippets.prompt: Assign an integer 10 to x, a float 3.14 to y and the text value to z, then print type() for each in one print call.
snippets.hint: type(value) returns the data type; pass all three inside a single print().
snippets.code:
x = 10
y = 3.14
z = "text"
print(type(x), type(y), type(z))
snippets.explain: Shows how Python classifies values. `10` is an int, `3.14` a float and `"text"` a str. `type()` reports the class of a value, so this prints three `<class ...>` objects and is the fastest way to debug a column that refuses to do maths.
snippets.gotcha: `type` needs the parentheses — `print(type(x))` works, `print(type x)` is a syntax error.

notes.note: An integer literal: a whole number, no decimal point.
A float literal: the decimal point makes it floating point.
A string literal: text inside quotes.
type() returns the data type of each value, all printed on one line.

snippets.title: Index into a list
snippets.prompt: Store three temperatures 21.5, 23.0 and 19.8 in a list called temperatures, then print the first element.
snippets.hint: Python lists are zero-indexed, so the first element is [0].
snippets.explain: Creates a list of three temperatures and prints the first one. Lists keep items in order and are written in square brackets. Indexing starts at 0, so `[0]` is the first element, `[1]` the second and `[-1]` the last.
snippets.gotcha: `temperatures[3]` raises IndexError — the valid positions here are 0, 1 and 2.

notes.note: A list literal: three floats in square brackets, separated by commas.
Square brackets after the list name select an element; 0 means the first item, so this prints 21.5.

snippets.title: Read a value from a dictionary
snippets.prompt: Create a dictionary student with keys "name" (value "Ada") and "score" (value 95), then print the score using square-bracket lookup.
snippets.hint: Use student["score"] with the key in double quotes.
snippets.explain: Builds a dictionary that maps keys to values and looks one value up by its key. Dictionaries are the Python shape of a single table row: field name → field value.
snippets.gotcha: `student[score]` without quotes looks for a variable named `score` and raises NameError.

notes.note: A dict literal with two key/value pairs: "name" → "Ada" and "score" → 95.
Look values up with dict[key], so this prints 95. The key must be spelled and quoted exactly.

snippets.title: Arithmetic and averages
snippets.prompt: Compute 10 + 5 * 2 into total, then divide total by 3 into mean and print mean.
snippets.hint: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so no brackets are needed.
snippets.explain: Demonstrates operator precedence and division. Multiplication happens before addition, so `10 + 5 * 2` is 20, not 30. Single `/` always returns a float, so the mean is 6.666…
snippets.gotcha: Use `//` for floor division or `round(x, 2)` when you want a tidy number in a report.

notes.note: `5 * 2` is evaluated first, then added to 10 — total becomes 20.
Single `/` performs true division and always returns a float.
Prints 6.666666666666667 rather than a rounded value.

snippets.title: Branch with if / elif / else
snippets.prompt: Set score to 82. Assign grade "A" when score is at least 90, "B" when at least 80, otherwise "C". Print grade.
snippets.hint: Use if / elif / else and the >= operator, then print(grade).
snippets.explain: Classifies a score into a letter grade using a chain of conditions. Python tests `if` first, then each `elif` in order, and runs only the first branch that is True; `else` is the fallback. The indented blocks are what makes each branch belong to its condition.
snippets.gotcha: Using `=` instead of `==` inside a condition is an assignment and raises a SyntaxError.

notes.note: The value being tested. Change it to 95 and the grade becomes A.
First test: is the score at least 90?
Runs only when the test above was True. Four spaces of indentation define the block.
Checked only if the first test failed; `>=` includes exactly 80.
80–89 lands here.
Catch-all branch when nothing above matched.
Scores below 80 get a C.
Printing outside the indented blocks shows the single grade that was assigned.

snippets.title: Loop over a range
snippets.prompt: Loop i from 0 to 4 with range(5) and print i raised to the power 2 on each iteration.
snippets.hint: Indent the body four spaces and use the exponent operator **.
snippets.explain: Repeats a block of code five times. `range(5)` yields 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five numbers, stopping before 5. Each pass binds the next number to `i`, and `**` raises it to the power of 2.
snippets.gotcha: `range(5)` gives 5 values starting at 0 — it does not include 5 itself.

notes.note: Loop header: `i` takes each value from range(5) in turn, and the colon opens the block.
The indented body runs once per value, printing 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 on separate lines.

snippets.title: Define a reusable mean function
snippets.prompt: Define a function mean(values) that returns the sum divided by the length, then print the mean of the list [2, 4, 6].
snippets.hint: Use sum() and len() inside a return statement; leave one blank line before the print.
snippets.explain: Defines a reusable function that computes an average, then calls it once. `def` names the function and lists its parameters; `return` sends a value back to the caller instead of printing it, which is what makes the function composable.
snippets.gotcha: Forgetting `return` makes the function hand back `None`, so `print` would show None.

notes.note: Function definition: the name `mean` and one parameter, `values`.
sum() adds the numbers, len() counts them, and the division returns the average to the caller.
Calls the function with the list [2, 4, 6]; the printed result is 4.0.

snippets.title: Collect rows in a list
snippets.prompt: Create an empty list called rows, then loop over the names Ada, Grace and Alan and append each name to rows. Print the list.
snippets.hint: Start with rows = [] and use a for loop over the literal list.
snippets.code:
rows = []
for name in ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan"]:
    rows.append(name)
print(rows)
snippets.explain: Grows a list one item at a time — the pattern behind building a table from scratch. It starts empty, loops over three names and appends each one, which is exactly how rows get accumulated before being turned into a DataFrame.
snippets.gotcha: `rows = rows.append(name)` sets rows to None — append changes the list in place and returns nothing.

notes.note: Starts with an empty list so append() has somewhere to add items.
Loops over a list literal of three names.
append() adds one item to the end of the list, growing it each pass.
Prints the completed list: ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Alan'].

snippets.title: Clone a repository and enter it
snippets.prompt: In the terminal, clone the repository https://github.com/user/project.git and then move into the project directory.
snippets.hint: Two commands: git clone <url> followed by cd project.
snippets.explain: Two terminal commands that get a project onto your machine: `git clone` downloads the repository together with its full commit history into a new folder, and `cd` moves your shell into that folder so later git commands act on it.
snippets.gotcha: Run `git status` after `cd` to confirm you are inside a repository before committing.

notes.note: Downloads the repository from the URL into a new local folder named after the repo (`project`).
Changes the working directory into that new folder.

snippets.title: Stage and commit a file
snippets.prompt: Stage the file data.csv and commit it with the message "Add raw dataset".
snippets.hint: git add <file> then git commit -m "<message>" — keep the message in double quotes.
snippets.code:
git add data.csv
git commit -m "Add raw dataset"
snippets.explain: The two-step save in git: `git add` stages the change (puts it in the next snapshot), and `git commit` records that snapshot with a message. Nothing is saved to history until the commit happens.
snippets.gotcha: `git commit` alone commits staged files only — a file you never `add`ed stays out of the snapshot.

notes.note: Stages `data.csv` — the file is now in the index, waiting to be committed.
Creates a commit of everything staged, labelled with the message "Add raw dataset". The -m flag takes the message inline.

snippets.title: Push to the remote
snippets.prompt: Push the current commits to the remote called origin on the branch main.
snippets.explain: Uploads local commits to the remote repository. The first argument is the remote name (`origin`, the default alias for the URL you cloned from) and the second is the branch you are pushing (`main`).
snippets.gotcha: If the remote has newer commits, the push is rejected — pull or rebase first.

notes.note: Sends the current branch's commits to the remote called origin, branch main.

snippets.title: Inspect repository state
snippets.prompt: Show the working tree status, then display the last five commits in one-line format.
snippets.hint: git status, then git log with the --oneline flag and -5.
snippets.explain: Read-only inspection. `git status` shows which files are modified, staged or untracked, and `git log --oneline -5` shows the five most recent commits in a compact one-line-per-commit format.
snippets.gotcha: `git log` can trap you in a pager — press q to return to the shell prompt.

notes.note: Reports the working tree state: staged, modified and untracked files.
--oneline compresses each commit to one line and -5 limits the output to the last five.

snippets.title: Install a package in Google Colab
snippets.prompt: In a Google Colab cell, install pandas with pip using the shell escape, then import it with the alias pd.
snippets.hint: Prefix the shell command with ! and import with the as alias.
snippets.code:
!pip install pandas
import pandas as pd
snippets.explain: In a Colab cell, a leading `!` runs the rest of the line as a shell command, so pip installs into the notebook's runtime. The import that follows uses `as` to give the library the conventional short alias.
snippets.gotcha: The pip install is not needed on a fresh Colab VM — pandas ships with it, so the line is often a no-op.

notes.note: The `!` escape runs this as a shell command on the Colab VM, not as Python.
Imports pandas under the alias pd, the alias every tutorial and the rest of this course uses.

snippets.title: Mount Google Drive in Colab
snippets.prompt: Mount your Google Drive in Colab by importing drive from google.colab and calling drive.mount on the path "/content/drive".
snippets.hint: from google.colab import drive, then drive.mount("/content/drive").
snippets.explain: Connects Colab to your Google Drive so files persist between sessions. `drive.mount` asks for authorisation and exposes your Drive under `/content/drive`, after which you can read CSVs with normal paths such as `/content/drive/MyDrive/data.csv`.
snippets.gotcha: Without mounting, the Colab VM is temporary — files you write disappear when the runtime resets.

notes.note: Imports just the `drive` helper from the google.colab package.
Mounts your Drive at the given path; Colab shows a consent prompt the first time.

snippets.title: Send a GET request
snippets.prompt: Import requests and fetch https://api.example.com/data with requests.get, storing the result in response. Print its status_code.
snippets.hint: Two lines of setup plus the call; leave a blank line before the request.
snippets.explain: Performs the simplest HTTP GET call. `requests.get` sends the request and returns a Response object; `status_code` is the HTTP status, where 200 means success and 4xx/5xx mean failure. Nothing is parsed yet — the body is still raw.
snippets.gotcha: A 404 or 500 does not raise an exception by default; you must check the status or call raise_for_status().

notes.note: Imports the third-party requests library, which wraps HTTP in one-line calls.
Sends a GET request to the URL and stores the whole Response object in `response`.
Prints the HTTP status code — 200 for a successful request.

snippets.title: Query parameters and error checking
snippets.prompt: Request the url stored in the variable url with the query parameter page set to 2, then raise an error for bad status codes.
snippets.explain: Sends query parameters and fails loudly on a bad response. `params=` builds `?page=2` for you and handles URL-encoding; `raise_for_status()` converts any 4xx/5xx status into an exception so broken data never silently flows into your pipeline.
snippets.gotcha: Never hand-build `url + '?page=2'` — encoding breaks as soon as a value contains a space or an ampersand.

notes.note: Passes the dict as query parameters, producing url?page=2 in the request.
Raises an HTTPError if the server answered with a client or server error status.

snippets.title: Parse a JSON response
snippets.prompt: Import json, parse response.text into a variable called payload, then print the first element of its items list.
snippets.hint: json.loads() converts text to Python objects; index with payload["items"][0].
snippets.explain: Turns the JSON text returned by an API into real Python objects. `json.loads` means “load string” and produces dicts and lists, which you then index like any other Python data — here the first element of the `items` list.
snippets.gotcha: `json.load` (no s) expects an already-open file object; `json.loads` expects text.

notes.note: Imports the standard-library json module (no installation needed).
Parses the response body text into Python dicts/lists. Note the s: loads = string in.
Indexes the parsed dict by key, then takes element 0 of that list.

snippets.title: Serialise a dict to JSON
snippets.prompt: Given a dictionary body with name "Ada" and score 95, print it as indented JSON with 2 spaces of indentation.
snippets.explain: Goes the other way: converts a Python dict into a JSON string. `indent=2` pretty-prints with two spaces per level, which makes the payload readable in logs or before POSTing it somewhere.
snippets.gotcha: Tuples become arrays and `None` becomes `null`; sets and DataFrames cannot be serialised directly.

notes.note: A normal Python dict — JSON objects and Python dicts look alike but are not the same thing.
json.dumps serialises it to text; indent=2 adds newlines and indentation for readability.

snippets.title: POST JSON to an API
snippets.prompt: Send the dictionary body to the variable url using requests.post as JSON, then print the parsed JSON reply from the response.
snippets.hint: Use the json= keyword argument, then response.json().
snippets.explain: Sends data to an API rather than asking for it. The `json=` keyword serialises the dict, sets the Content-Type header to application/json and attaches it as the request body. `response.json()` parses the reply straight into Python objects.
snippets.gotcha: Using `data=body` sends form-encoded text, not JSON, which many APIs reject with 415 or 400.

notes.note: POSTs the dict as a JSON body — do not json.dumps it yourself when using the json= keyword.
Parses the response body in one step instead of calling json.loads(response.text).

snippets.title: Parse HTML with BeautifulSoup
snippets.prompt: Import BeautifulSoup from bs4, parse the html string with the "html.parser" parser into soup, then print the page title text.
snippets.hint: soup.title.get_text() extracts the text of the title tag.
snippets.code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
print(soup.title.get_text())
snippets.explain: Parses an HTML page into a searchable tree. BeautifulSoup needs the markup plus a parser name; after that you navigate with `.title`, `.find` and `.find_all` instead of regexes. `get_text()` strips the tags and returns just the visible text.
snippets.gotcha: BeautifulSoup does not fetch pages — pass it `requests.get(url).text` first.

notes.note: Imports only the BeautifulSoup class from the bs4 package.
Parses the HTML string and returns a navigable tree; html.parser is the built-in, dependency-free parser.
Walks to the title tag and prints its inner text without any markup.

snippets.title: Extract table rows
snippets.prompt: Loop over every tr element in soup and build a list of the stripped text of each td cell inside that row.
snippets.hint: Use find_all("tr") then a list comprehension over row.find_all("td") with get_text(strip=True).
snippets.code:
for row in soup.find_all("tr"):
    cells = [c.get_text(strip=True) for c in row.find_all("td")]
snippets.explain: Walks an HTML table. `find_all("tr")` returns every table row, and for each row a list comprehension collects the text of its `td` cells. `strip=True` removes the surrounding whitespace and newlines that HTML formatting leaves behind, which is essential for clean data.
snippets.gotcha: Without `strip=True` you get values like '\n    42\n  ' which break numeric conversion later.

notes.note: Loops over every table-row element in the document.
List comprehension: for each cell in this row, take the stripped text, producing one string per column.

snippets.title: Cache API results to disk
snippets.prompt: Write the payload dictionary to data.json as indented JSON with 2-space indentation, using a with block and a file handle named f.
snippets.hint: Open with open("data.json", "w") and use json.dump(payload, f, indent=2).
snippets.code:
with open("data.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(payload, f, indent=2)
snippets.explain: Caches an API payload as a local JSON file so you do not re-fetch it every run. `with open(...)` closes the file automatically even if an error occurs, and `json.dump` writes the Python object straight into that open file handle.
snippets.gotcha: `json.dump` writes to a file handle; `json.dumps` returns a string — mixing them up corrupts the file.

notes.note: Opens data.json for writing ("w" overwrites) and binds the handle to `f` for the indented block.
json.dump (no s) writes into the open file object, pretty-printed with two spaces.

snippets.title: Tidy rows as a list of dicts
snippets.prompt: Build a list called rows holding two dictionaries: city "KL" with temp 32, and city "SG" with temp 30. Then print the city of the first row.
snippets.hint: One dictionary per line, trailing comma between them.
snippets.explain: The canonical tidy-data shape: a list where every dictionary is one row and every key is one column. All rows share the same keys, which is exactly what `pd.DataFrame(rows)` expects, and you address a single cell as `rows[row_index][column_name]`.
snippets.gotcha: Rows with different key names become NaN-filled columns once converted to a DataFrame.

notes.note: Opens a list literal; the entries are dictionaries, one per row.
First row: city "KL" with temp 32.
Second row, same keys in the same order — consistent keys are what makes it tidy.
Closes the list.
Row 0, then the "city" key of that row, printing KL.

snippets.title: Pull one column into a list
snippets.prompt: Using a list comprehension over rows, collect every row's "temp" value into temps, then print the average of temps.
snippets.hint: [row["temp"] for row in rows], then sum(temps) / len(temps).
snippets.code:
temps = [row["temp"] for row in rows]
print(sum(temps) / len(temps))
snippets.explain: Extracts one column out of the row list, then summarises it. The list comprehension visits each row and keeps only the `temp` value, turning row-oriented data into a plain list you can run maths on.
snippets.gotcha: A comprehension already builds the list — do not wrap it in another pair of square brackets.

notes.note: Comprehension: for every row, take row["temp"] — result is [32, 30].
sum()/len() is the manual way to compute a mean; the printed result is 31.0.

snippets.title: Column-oriented storage
snippets.prompt: Build a dictionary called columns mapping the key city to the list ["KL", "SG"] and temp to the list [32, 30], then print the number of cities.
snippets.explain: The column-oriented alternative to a list of rows: one dict, one key per column, each value a list of that column's entries. Arrow-style tools and APIs often hand data back in this shape, and NumPy/pandas love it because each column is contiguous.
snippets.gotcha: The lists must be the same length — a short column silently produces misaligned rows.

notes.note: Two columns: "city" holds two strings, "temp" holds two numbers, positionally aligned.
Counts the entries in the city column, printing 2.

snippets.title: Unique values with a set
snippets.prompt: Create a set called cities containing "KL", "SG" and a repeated "KL", then print how many unique values it holds.
snippets.hint: Sets drop duplicates automatically; use len().
snippets.explain: Sets store only unique values, so duplicates collapse on creation. This is the quickest way to answer “how many distinct categories are in this column?” without loading pandas.
snippets.gotcha: Sets are unordered, so you cannot index them with [0] — use `sorted(cities)[0]` instead.

notes.note: "KL" appears twice in the literal but the set keeps it once, so the set is {"KL", "SG"}.
len() on a set counts unique members, printing 2.

snippets.title: Tuple unpacking
snippets.prompt: Unpack the tuple (1, 2) into variables first and second, then print their sum.
snippets.hint: first, second = (1, 2) on a single line.
snippets.explain: Unpacks a tuple into named variables in a single assignment. Python matches positions on the left to values on the right, which is the same mechanism `for index, row in df.iterrows()` relies on.
snippets.gotcha: The counts must match: three names for a two-item tuple raises ValueError.

notes.note: Two targets, two values — first gets 1, second gets 2.
Adds them and prints 3.

snippets.title: Count categories with defaultdict
snippets.prompt: Import defaultdict from collections, create counts with int as the default factory, count the values in the list ["KL", "SG", "KL"] by incrementing counts[city], then print counts.
snippets.hint: defaultdict(int) starts every missing key at 0.
snippets.code:
from collections import defaultdict

counts = defaultdict(int)
for city in ["KL", "SG", "KL"]:
    counts[city] += 1
print(counts)
snippets.explain: Counts how often each value occurs without an `if key in counts` check. `defaultdict(int)` invents a default of 0 the first time a key is seen, so `+= 1` always works. This is the manual version of `df["city"].value_counts()`.
snippets.gotcha: A plain `{}` raises KeyError on `counts[city] += 1` the first time a value appears.

notes.note: Imports defaultdict from the standard-library collections module.
A dict whose missing keys default to int() — that is, 0.
Loops over three city values, one of which repeats.
First sighting of a key starts at 0, so this becomes 1; the repeat reaches 2.
Prints defaultdict(<class 'int'>, {'KL': 2, 'SG': 1}).

snippets.title: Sort rows by a column
snippets.prompt: Sort the list rows in place by the "temp" key in descending order using a lambda key function.
snippets.explain: Sorts the row list in place by a field. `key=` names the value to sort on (here a lambda that pulls `row["temp"]`), and `reverse=True` puts the largest first. `list.sort()` mutates the list and returns None, unlike `sorted()` which returns a new list.
snippets.gotcha: `rows = rows.sort(...)` assigns None — either call sort() alone or use sorted(rows, ...).

notes.note: Sorts rows by the "temp" value, highest first. The lambda receives one row and returns its sort key.

snippets.title: Load a CSV into a DataFrame
snippets.prompt: Import pandas as pd, load "data.csv" into a DataFrame called df, then print its shape.
snippets.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
print(df.shape)
snippets.explain: The entry point of nearly every pandas workflow: read a CSV into a DataFrame. `pd.read_csv` infers column names from the header and dtypes from the values; `df.shape` then reports (rows, columns), the fastest sanity check that the file loaded as expected.
snippets.gotcha: A FileNotFoundError here almost always means the notebook's working directory is not where the CSV lives.

notes.note: Imports pandas under the universal alias pd.
Reads data.csv from the working directory into a DataFrame called df.
shape is a tuple (n_rows, n_cols), e.g. (1000, 5).

snippets.title: Preview the top and bottom rows
snippets.prompt: Print the first five rows of df, then the last three rows.
snippets.hint: df.head() defaults to five rows; df.tail(3) gives three.
snippets.explain: Sneak-peeks the frame. `head()` shows the first five rows and `tail(3)` the last three — useful for checking that the column names parsed correctly and that totals or trailing junk are not sitting at the end of the file.
snippets.gotcha: head()/tail() only display — they do not modify df.

notes.note: First five rows, with the index on the left and every column across.
Passing 3 overrides the default of five, giving the last three rows.

snippets.title: Inspect schema and dtypes
snippets.prompt: Print a concise schema summary of df that shows column names, non-null counts and dtypes.
snippets.explain: Prints a compact schema report: index range, every column name, how many non-null values it has and its dtype, plus memory usage. It is the one call that tells you whether a column is numeric or accidentally text, and whether gaps exist.
snippets.gotcha: If a numeric column shows `object`, some value in it is text — often a comma or a blank string.

notes.note: Prints the schema summary. Read the Dtype column: `object` means text, so maths will fail.

snippets.title: Select a column
snippets.prompt: Store the "temp" column of df in temps, then print its maximum value.
snippets.hint: df["temp"] selects a Series; .max() reduces it.
snippets.explain: Selects a single column, which pandas returns as a Series (one dimension), then reduces it to a single number with `.max()`. `df["temp"]` with one pair of brackets is a column; `df[["temp"]]` with two would return a one-column DataFrame.
snippets.gotcha: `df[temp]` without quotes looks for a variable named temp and raises NameError.

notes.note: Single brackets select the column named "temp" and return a Series.
max() reduces that whole Series to its largest value.

snippets.title: Filter rows with a condition
snippets.prompt: Keep only the rows of df where "temp" is greater than 30, store them in hot, then print the first five rows of hot.
snippets.explain: Boolean filtering: `df["temp"] > 30` produces a True/False Series, and using that inside `df[...]` keeps only the rows where it is True. Chain `.head()` to eyeball the survivors instead of printing thousands of rows.
snippets.gotcha: The mask must come from the same DataFrame and the same index — compare df to df, not to a filtered copy.

notes.note: The comparison builds a boolean mask; df[mask] returns only the rows where it is True.
Shows the first five matching rows.

snippets.title: Combine two filter conditions
snippets.prompt: Select the rows of df where "temp" is above 30 AND "city" equals "KL", wrapping each condition in brackets and joining them with an ampersand.

import pandas as pd
